transcript.text: Hello and welcome.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: My name’s Heather McCallum and I’m one of the potters who work here at Edelman Pottery.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Before we go into the workshop, I just want to say a bit about the craft of pottery.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Then we’ll have a look at the equipment and you can try making a pot of your own.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Like many people, I’m sure you know that pottery as an art form is tens of thousands of years old.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: And we know this because it stands the test of time.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Things like baskets and pictures don’t survive in the earth in the same way that pots do. and even if ancient pots are found in small pieces they still provide a lot of information about the past.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: There's no doubt that pottery has given archaeologists a fascinating insight into how ancient humans lived.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: The shape of an artefact may have been lost but archaeologists can tell whether the pots were for, say, storage or cooking by examining the impressions on the clay, the scratches from tools, and the clay itself can reveal where the pots came from.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: When I ask people why they want to take a pottery class with me, they sometimes talk about these things.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Like our ancestors, they hope that something they create will also last longer than they do, that their work, whether it is good or not, might say something about humanity many years after their death.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Of course, you will all have your own reasons for coming here.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: As far as I’m concerned, what I love most is the concentration you need to make a good pot.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: That focus takes you away from the stresses of everyday life.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: If you’re elderly, it’s also good exercise for hands and wrists and helps with arthritis.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: And of course, it’s a fun activity for children because it’s so messy.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Here at Edelman Pottery, we show you some of the basic pottery techniques so that you can use these to create whatever you wish.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: A gift for a friend, perhaps.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Like nearly everyone who comes here, I’m sure this is the first time you will have tried the art So we’ll keep things simple today Now, before we move on, can I just say a word about what you’re wearing?
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: As we said in our email please remove any watches necklaces etc and put them somewhere safe If you have long hair do tie it back now We provide aprons later but I trust your clothes are old but comfortable not your favourite T-shirt or jeans.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: So now we’re in the workshop.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Have a look around.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: There’s a lot going on.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: To make pottery that will last, you need a potter’s wheel, a kiln, which is basically a very hot oven where you fire the pottery, and some tools.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: So, first, the kiln.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: If you look over in the far corner, you’ll see one of ours.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Since their invention, kilns have changed very little, though in the past 20 years a lot of progress has been made in temperature control.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Basically, a kiln removes the water from clay at temperatures of around 1000 degrees Celsius.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: This allows anything you’ve made to set permanently in shape.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: It’s a pretty ugly heavy object that’s hard to keep in a house or flat, so most people don’t have one.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: You may think, can’t I use my oven?
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Well, that’s possible, but domestic ovens don’t really get hot enough and eventually the clay will crack and fall apart.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Some people fire pottery in a fire pit outside but bear in mind… that can be dangerous You also need to know about safety procedures for kilns as they release toxic compounds into the air Every potter needs a potter’s wheel.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: This machine is used to shape the clay into an object with circular walls or sides, such as a bowl.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Its invention revolutionised the pottery industry, allowing multiple items to be produced in a day.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Lastly, there are a number of different tools that potters use, depending on what they want to make.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: When you start, your hands can make all kinds of shapes and curves without relying on a sculpting tool.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: However, there are some basic tools that you will need to handle the clay on the wheel.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Some look very strange and have even odder names that you may find hard to remember.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: Rather than go through them all now, I’ll just name a few tools as we go along.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: We can provide these and I wouldn’t recommend spending money on them yet.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: So, let’s try making a pot of your own.
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: If you sit down…
transcript.speaker: HEATHER

transcript.text: It’s quite hard to think of a city that doesn’t have a big river running through it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: If you think about the major cities in the world, Shanghai, New York, Mumbai, London, they’re nearly all built on rivers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: When these cities were established hundreds or even thousands of years ago, the rivers were a big part of people’s lives.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In 16th century London, the quickest way to get from one part of the city to another was by river.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But people also used the river for fishing, as the water then was relatively clean, and they would also go on boat trips up and down the river just for pleasure, as a relaxing escape from the noise and bustle of the city streets But as industries developed and populations increased city rivers suffered The rising number of people meant there was a huge increase in the amount of sewage discharged into the rivers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Rivers had always been used for this purpose, but when the number of inhabitants was so small, that wasn’t such a problem.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, as cities grew to over a million inhabitants, the impact on the rivers became more serious.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In addition, other types of pollution increased, as factories were built beside the river and discharged their waste materials into the water.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This got worse over time.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As recently as 1957, scientists at London’s Natural History Museum declared that the River Thames was dead in biological terms, as the water was too filthy to support any kind of life.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But in recent years, as rivers lost their industrial function, cities have begun to recognise their true value and to take steps to clean them up.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, the River Thames is now cleaner than it’s been for 150 years.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These days you can see seals swimming in the water, and recently people had to try to rescue a whale, which had got lost and swum up the river from the sea by mistake.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Unfortunately, they didn’t succeed, but the problem was disorientation rather than the quality of the water.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Then, all around the world, riverside areas are now seen as prime sites for development.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Warehouses that were once used for storing goods are now being converted into expensive restaurants and also into apartments with river views, which are in great demand and sell for astronomical prices.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In Los Angeles, on the west coast of the USA, an architect has plans to revitalise the banks of the river and to make a park there which can provide facilities for sports as well as a natural environment for relaxing in It's also hoped that the riverside can be used for other purposes It’s been proposed that facilities could be provided for displaying projects related to various kinds of art that have been produced by local people, for example.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In the city of Paris, During the summer months of July and August, all the traffic is banned from the roads by the sides of the river, and the banks are transformed into beaches, where people can relax in deck chairs under potted palm trees, sunbathe or buy a drink or a snack while enjoying the view.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But to make the most of our rivers in our increasingly crowded cities, we need to allow them to regain their original purpose and be used as a means of transport, reclaiming our streets from cars and lorries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: To do this, we’ll have to shift more traffic back to the river, but this time cleanly and silently, making the most of modern technology.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Already, more than two billion passengers use the ferry to travel in cities around the world, like Istanbul, San Francisco and New York, and these numbers are set to rise further.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Admittedly, it’s not a fast way of travelling, but neither is a car when it’s stuck in traffic.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Of course, passenger traffic on roads might decrease as more people start working from home, but another recent development, the huge rise in online shopping, has meant that another form of urban traffic just keeps on growing, and that’s deliveries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Trucks and vans in the city pollute and double-park while dropping off parcels.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Imagine using the immense capacity of shipping to take these trucks off the road One freight barge can replace 44 large trucks uses far less energy and causes less pollution When the barge docks at the riverside the parcels could be taken the last few kilometres to their final destination on cargo bikes, electric ones of course.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is already happening in the Dutch city of Amsterdam, and in future the final stage could even be carried out by drone, although at present this isn’t allowed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Wouldn’t it be great to unblock our city centres in this way?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Looking further ahead…
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
